name: Olga Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small studio of six that does a lot of print. Labels for a honey farm and a cheese maker, the furniture shop's catalogue twice a year, menus, that sort of thing. Today I'm getting the cheese labels ready for the printer, checking the colours and the cut lines so nothing gets wasted. Once a month I go down to the print works on the industrial estate to watch the first sheets come off the press.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a jar of honey with my label is sitting in the farm shop. It's real, you can pick it up. What wears me out is clients who change the text after it's gone to print, and a wage that's on the low side. My boyfriend Marek is an electrician, and between us we've got about three weeks of money spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with the cheese labels. I'm not someone who posts opinions. At work I'd just say I'm glad nothing big changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure my job is that safe anyway. Print orders have been dropping for years as more things go online. The furniture shop already cut their catalogue from sixty pages to forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and not touch the AI stuff, since there'd be no need. I'd try to put a bit aside each month, maybe forty. And I'd keep my eye on the job board for the print works, in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just aware the print side is slowly shrinking under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the furniture catalogue goes fully online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the studio loses its biggest print job, and I'm the print person. I'd probably end up doing website banners, which I'm not great at. My boss Petra, who owns the studio, has said as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you try the AI tools in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Petra told me to, I'd try. But I'm slow with new software and I don't trust it with colours. A wrong colour on ten thousand labels is a disaster.

say: I'd say **that's that** and get on with the work.
I'd tell colleagues I'm **glad** nothing big changed.
think: Print orders have been **dropping** for years as things go online.
The furniture catalogue already fell from **sixty pages to forty**.
do: Carry on and **avoid** the AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware the **print side** is shrinking under her.
S0.quote: A wrong colour on ten thousand labels is a disaster.
fieldNote: Olga's pressure comes from **print decline**, not AI.
She's the studio's **print specialist**, which is both her value and her risk.
She distrusts AI on **colour accuracy**, a practical rather than political objection.

steps.text: Keep preparing labels and catalogues for print
Put aside forty a month into savings
Check the print works job board every few weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use what saves money, but someone still has to check it. I'd say that at work, because it's true. I wouldn't argue about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the studio would cut a designer, and it could be me. I'm average and I don't use the tools, and the others do a bit. My print knowledge helps, but labels and layouts are exactly what the software gets good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Petra plainly what she plans, so I'm not surprised. I'd cut the takeaway nights and the car insurance extras, which saves about sixty a month. And I'd ask the print works if they need someone in prepress, getting files ready for the press, since I already know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd rather know the bad news than wait for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather know. What would Petra probably say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say nothing's decided, which means it is. She's kind but she has a business to run. I'd want a date, not a feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the print works and not another studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there isn't another studio within forty minutes. The print works is half machines and half people standing next to them. That feels like it lasts a bit longer.

say: I'd say using what **saves money** is sensible, but someone must **check** it.
think: The studio would cut a designer, and **it could be me**.
Labels and layouts are what the **software** gets good at.
do: Ask Petra (the studio owner) **directly** about her plans.
Cut takeaways and car extras to save **sixty a month**.
Ask the print works about a **prepress** job.
S1.quote: There isn't another studio within forty minutes. The print works is half machines and half people standing next to them.
fieldNote: Olga is **matter-of-fact** and doesn't blame anyone.
She sees herself as **likely to be cut**, partly because she avoids the tools.
Her fallback is **prepress** at the print works, using skills she already has.

steps.text: Cut takeaway nights and car insurance extras, saving sixty a month
Ask the print works about a prepress job
Ask Petra for a clear date before deciding anything else

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened faster than anyone was ready for, and the government should help people through it. Not forever, just to get to the next thing. I'd say it plainly, without shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the studio closes or shrinks to Petra and a laptop within a year. My design work is thinking and screen work, so it goes straight away. The press side lasts until the robots, around 2031. That's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the print works the first week and take whatever they offer, even packing or running the guillotine. Marek and I would move somewhere cheaper, maybe the flat above his brother's garage. And I'd stop every subscription and the gym the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't do well with fast change, and this is the fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marek's work look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's an electrician, so he's in houses, under floors, in roof spaces. He'd probably be fine until the robots, and maybe a bit after. So he'd carry us, which I'd hate but accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the honey jars in the farm shop. Sounds silly. The machine would make the labels and nobody would know a person ever did.

say: I'd say it came **faster** than anyone was ready for.
Government should **help people** across to the next thing.
think: The studio closes or shrinks to **Petra and a laptop**.
The **press side** lasts until about 2031, so that's where I'd go.
do: Take **any job** at the print works in the first week.
Move to the **cheaper flat** above Marek's brother's garage.
S2.quote: My design work is thinking and screen work, so it goes straight away. The press side lasts until the robots, around 2031.
fieldNote: Olga reads the **robot gap** clearly and plans to use it.
She'd rely on **Marek's income**, which she says she'd hate but accept.
Her sense of loss is about **pride** in physical work, like labels on jars.

steps.text: Take any job at the print works, even packing
Move to the flat above Marek's brother's garage
Cancel every subscription and the gym the same day
Lean on Marek's electrician wage for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's be sensible about it. Companies should give notice, and colleges should offer short courses. I'd say that at work and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd move to the print works in the next two years, before everyone else tries to. Press work lasts until about 2034. That gives me time to learn to run the machines properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the print works for Saturday shifts to learn the press. I'd put sixty a month away and not touch it. And I'd stay at the studio until Petra says otherwise, because the wage is steady for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. I like having a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After 2034, when the robots reach the press, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe I'd be one of the people who looks after the machines. Marek says electricians will be needed to wire it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools at the studio before you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Learning the AI tools at the studio would just speed up my own exit. I'd rather spend the effort on the press.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **plan sensibly**.
Companies should give **notice** and colleges should run short courses.
think: I'd move to the **print works** within two years.
Press work lasts until about **2034**, giving time to learn.
do: Work **Saturday shifts** at the print works to learn the press.
Put **sixty a month** away and leave it.
Stay at the studio while the **wage** lasts.
feel: **Anxious** but **organised**, because she likes a list.
S3.quote: Learning the AI tools at the studio would just speed up my own exit. I'd rather spend the effort on the press.
fieldNote: Olga uses the warning to move **early**, before others crowd the print works.
She refuses AI tools as **pointless**, not on principle.
She has **no plan** after 2034 and admits it.

steps.text: Work Saturday shifts at the print works learning the press
Put sixty a month into savings and leave it alone
Stay at Petra's studio while the wage is steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people will adapt. That's the sensible line. I'd say it to friends who panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough for me to shift over to the print works without a crisis. But the print works itself might not survive another ten years of things going online. So I'm not as relaxed as I sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change nothing this year except saving a bit more. In two or three years I'd start the press shifts. I'd also ask Marek about helping with his paperwork and quotes, in case we ever ran something together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. The kind you notice at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change nothing this year. Is that a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's how I am. I wait until I can see the thing clearly. With ten years I think I can afford to wait one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home with Marek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a flat. With ten years of warning, maybe we still would, but smaller, near his work. I wouldn't sign a mortgage on my design wage.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and people will adapt.
I'd say that to **panicking friends**, because it's the sensible line.
think: Ten years is enough to move to the **print works**.
The print works might not survive ten more years of **online** shift.
do: Change nothing this year except **saving more**.
Start **press shifts** in two or three years.
feel: Quietly **anxious**, the kind she notices **at night**.
S4.quote: I wouldn't sign a mortgage on my design wage.
fieldNote: She **waits** until things are clear, and a decade lets her.
A **flat purchase** shrinks and moves near Marek's work.

steps.text: Wait a year before starting press shifts
Save a bit more each month this year
Buy a smaller flat near Marek's work instead

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I need time, and that one gives none. What would help is short, cheap courses for jobs like press operator, and a bit of income support while you're between things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how long people like me take to change. I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with new things. Give me time and I'll get there.

headlineQuote: I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with new things. Give me time and I'll get there.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old print designer** at a six-person studio, on low pay.
She never uses AI and distrusts it on **practical** grounds, like colour accuracy.
Her plan in every picture is to move to the local **print works**.
She is **matter-of-fact** and blames no one, but needs time more than anything.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she needs time and it gives **none**.
whatWouldHelp: Short, cheap **courses** for jobs like press operator, plus **income support** between jobs.
